name: IBPS PO
fullName: Institute of Banking Personnel Selection – Common Recruitment Process for Probationary Officers/Management Trainees (CRP PO/MT)
approxCandidates: ≈10–11 lakh applicants; ≈6–7 lakh appear in prelims (recent cycles, unofficial estimates)
eligibility: Graduate in any discipline; 20–30 years (age relaxation for reserved categories)

notification.summary: CRP PO/MT-XVI (2026) is in progress: prelims were held on 22–23 Aug 2026, the prelims result was declared on 23 Sep 2026 and the mains was held on 4 Oct 2026; interviews are next. Vacancies were reported as ≈7,500+ (initially 6,715, later revised per news reports). The official ibps.in site could not be reached from the research environment, so dates are taken from multiple news/education portals.

importantDates.date: 21 Jul 2026 (some portals report an extension to 26 Jul)

pattern.notes: Separate 20-minute timer for each section (no switching). Sectional and overall cut-offs apply; prelims is qualifying only and its marks are not counted for the final merit. Scores are normalised across shifts. Mains (objective + descriptive) and interview follow (final merit 80:20).

trendAnalysis.summary: Since the 2025 cycle the prelims has 30 English + 35 Quant + 35 Reasoning questions with 20-minute sectional timing. Overall difficulty has been moderate (good attempts ≈63–74 in 2026). Reasoning is dominated by puzzles and seating arrangements (≈15–18 questions, often floor/box/month puzzles with two variables) plus syllogism, inequality and small misc topics. Quant is the toughest section: 2–3 DI sets (table, bar/line, caselet) and arithmetic word problems have replaced much of the old simplification; quadratic equations and number series (often wrong-number) appear in most shifts. English leans on one long RC (7–10 Qs), cloze, error spotting, fillers and rearrangement; word-swap and phrase-replacement formats are rising.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from shift-wise memory-based analyses of IBPS PO prelims 2024 (Oct 2024) and 2025 (23–24 Aug 2025) published by coaching sites (Time4Education, Physics Wallah, Adda247, Career Power), checked against the official IBPS prelims pattern. The 2026 prelims had not been analysed in detail at the time of compilation, so archetypes are backed by 2024 and 2025 only. Patterns are paraphrased; no real question is reproduced.

archetypes.pattern: RC set (350–450 words, economy/banking/technology/environment theme): identify the central idea or main argument; distractors are true-but-partial details or over-generalisations
RC fact-check: 'Which of the following is true / NOT true according to the passage' — one option distorts a qualifier (some→most, may→will) or reverses cause and effect
RC inference with statements I, II, III and combination options (Only I / Only I and III …); the trap statement overstates what the passage says
RC vocabulary-in-context: synonym or antonym of a word used in the passage, with distractors that are dictionary meanings not fitting the context
RC purpose/tone/title: why the author mentions a detail, the author's tone, or the most suitable title
Passage cloze with numbered blanks; five same-part-of-speech options where distractors are look-alike or collocation-breaking words
Cloze with a bold word already in each blank: choose the correct replacement or 'No replacement required'
Sentence split into parts (A)–(D) plus 'No error' (E); errors in subject–verb agreement, prepositions, pronouns, tense, comparatives, or inversion after negative adverbs
Choose the grammatically correct (or incorrect) sentence among five similar sentences on one theme
Double filler: two blanks in one sentence, five word-pairs where one word of each wrong pair fits but the other does not
Single filler: one blank, five words close in meaning; only one matches the tone/collocation of the sentence
Para jumble of five or six sentences on one theme; choose the correct order (options are sequences); connectors like 'however', 'as a result' and pronouns fix the order
Para jumble asking which sentence comes FIRST / THIRD / LAST after rearrangement (options are sentence letters)
Word swap: four highlighted words in a sentence; identify the pair whose interchange makes the sentence correct, or 'No interchange required'
Phrase replacement: a highlighted phrase with a grammar/idiom error; choose the correct replacement, or 'No replacement required'
Standalone synonym/antonym of a moderately advanced word; distractors include words of the opposite sense
Table DI (5 rows × 2–3 columns): percentage increase/decrease of one entity between two years, or one entity as a percentage of another
Table DI with a percentage column (e.g. share of a sub-category): compute derived values (sum, average, difference or ratio of derived quantities)
Caselet DI: a paragraph giving a total and splits in ratios/percentages; questions combine two splits or ask what changes after a transfer
Pie-chart DI (shares in % or degrees of a total): find values, differences and ratios across sectors
Bar/line-graph DI (values given for 5–6 categories or months): averages, ratios and percentage differences
Two quadratic equations in x and y with integer/fraction roots; compare x and y using the five standard relations (> ≥ < ≤ / cannot be established)
Missing number series built on differences of squares/cubes, alternate ×n +k, or ×n with increasing n
Wrong number series: one term breaks the ×/+ pattern; find it
Exact simplification with BODMAS, percentages, fractions, squares and square roots; find '?'
Approximation: decimals close to whole numbers in %, ×, ÷, √ and powers; find the nearest value
Profit & loss with marked price, discount and cost price (single or successive discounts, 'had he sold for ₹x more')
Percentage word problem: income–expenditure–savings, successive percentage change, or one value as a percentage of another
Partnership with unequal times or a mid-year change of capital; find a partner's share of profit
Ages: present-age ratio with a condition some years before/after; find an age or sum of ages
Ratio & proportion: dividing an amount in a ratio, or changing a ratio by adding/removing a quantity
Time & work / pipes: efficiencies combined, one leaves after some days, or an emptying pipe
Trains crossing poles/platforms/each other, relative speed, or average speed of a round trip
Boats and streams: downstream/upstream speeds and times
Simple vs compound interest: CI–SI difference, amount at CI, or a sum split between two rates
Mixture & alligation: mixing two varieties to a target price/ratio, or adding/replacing liquid
Probability with balls/cards/committees, using combinations
Mensuration: rectangle/circle/cylinder area, perimeter or volume relationships
Linear row (7–9 persons, all facing one direction), sometimes with vacant seats or an attribute; 3–5 questions on positions, neighbours and 'how many between'
Linear arrangement with mixed directions (some face north, some south) or two parallel rows facing each other
Circular table (6–8 persons) facing the centre (or some outside); left/right relations and 'second to the left of' questions
Floor-based puzzle (5–8 floors, sometimes two flats per floor) with a second attribute such as colour/city/fruit
Scheduling puzzle: persons/events on days of the week or months (sometimes with dates 1xth/2xth); 'how many between' questions
Box stacking: boxes placed one above another, with colour/item attribute and 'how many boxes between' clues
Comparison puzzle: heights/weights/marks of 5–6 persons with 'more than only' clues; ask rank or a derived value
Syllogism with 2–3 statements and two conclusions, including 'possibility' conclusions; standard five options
Syllogism with 'Only a few' or 'No' statements where a definite 'All' conclusion is the trap
Direct inequality: two or three combined statements, two conclusions to check
Inequality where the conclusions form a complementary pair (A > B / A = B) and the answer is 'Either I or II follows'
Blood relation chain or 'pointing to a photograph' statement; gender ambiguity is the usual trap
Coded blood relation: symbols (+, −, ×, ÷ or @, #) denote relations; decode an expression
Direction & distance: a person walks a path with left/right turns; find the shortest distance and direction from start
Point-based direction: several points given relative to each other; find direction/distance between two of them
Letter coding: word coded by letter shifts / reversal / opposite letters; code a new word
Sentence (Chinese) coding: three or four phrases coded in two-letter codes; find the code of a word by elimination
Order & ranking: positions from both ends of a row/class, total count, or persons between two people
Alphanumeric-symbol arrangement: count elements satisfying a 'preceded by / followed by' condition, or find the nth element from an end
Letter pairs in a word with as many letters between them as in the English alphabet
Number formation: digits of 3-digit numbers rearranged/operated on; find the resulting number or difference
Data sufficiency with two statements on seating/coding/blood relation; standard five options

resources.notes: IBPS does not publish full question papers or answer keys; candidates can view their own scorecards on ibps.in. IBPS posts an 'Information Handout' with sample questions for each CRP and offers a short online practice test before each exam. Memory-based previous papers are compiled by coaching portals and are unofficial.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Over the past decade, India's approach to digital public infrastructure has rested on a simple idea: build open, interoperable rails and let many players compete on top of them. A unique digital identity lowered the cost of verifying customers, while a real-time payment system allowed even small merchants to accept money without expensive card terminals. The results have been striking. Transactions that once required a branch visit can now be completed on a basic smartphone in seconds. Yet access is not the same as empowerment. Many first-time users still rely on a relative to complete payments, and a single fraudulent call can wipe out savings that took years to build. Analysts therefore argue that the next phase must focus less on adding users and more on building trust — through simple grievance redress, clear disclosure of charges and sustained financial-literacy campaigns. Without such safeguards, the very ease that drew millions into the formal system could, paradoxically, push some of them back towards cash.

Which of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?
options: Digital payments have failed to reach small merchants
Digital rails have widened access, but the next priority should be building users' trust and safety
Cash is safer than digital payments for first-time users
Digital identity has made bank branches unnecessary
Financial-literacy campaigns have already solved the problem of fraud
questions.explanation: The passage praises the reach of digital rails but says 'access is not the same as empowerment' and that the next phase must focus on building trust.

relevance.note: DPI/UPI economy passage with central-idea Q; distractors are partial/over-general claims as in PO 2024 RC

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Over the past decade, India's approach to digital public infrastructure has rested on a simple idea: build open, interoperable rails and let many players compete on top of them. A unique digital identity lowered the cost of verifying customers, while a real-time payment system allowed even small merchants to accept money without expensive card terminals. The results have been striking. Transactions that once required a branch visit can now be completed on a basic smartphone in seconds. Yet access is not the same as empowerment. Many first-time users still rely on a relative to complete payments, and a single fraudulent call can wipe out savings that took years to build. Analysts therefore argue that the next phase must focus less on adding users and more on building trust — through simple grievance redress, clear disclosure of charges and sustained financial-literacy campaigns. Without such safeguards, the very ease that drew millions into the formal system could, paradoxically, push some of them back towards cash.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
I. Ease of use alone does not guarantee that people will keep using digital payments.
II. Fraud has already pushed most users back to cash.
III. Lower costs of verifying customers helped digital services spread.
questions.explanation: I follows from the last sentence (ease could push some back to cash); III follows from 'lowered the cost of verifying customers'. II overstates — the passage says it 'could' push 'some' users back.

relevance.note: I/II/III inference combo with 'most users' overstatement trap, exactly PO RC style

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.
Neither the manager nor his assistants (A)/ was present at the meeting (B)/ that was called to discuss (C)/ the quarterly results. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: With 'neither…nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'assistants' (plural), so 'was' should be 'were'. Error in part B.

relevance.note: Neither-nor proximity agreement split A-E, a staple PO error-spotting item

questions.question:
Choose the pair of words that best fills both blanks.
The new policy is expected to ______ private investment, but critics fear it may ______ the fiscal deficit.
questions.explanation: 'But critics fear' signals a contrast: the policy is expected to do something good (spur investment) while critics fear something bad (widen the deficit).

relevance.note: Double filler with half-fitting pairs (curb/narrow etc.) matching PO 2024 double-filler style

questions.question:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Despite repeated warnings from the traffic police, he remained ______ to the danger and continued to drive recklessly.
questions.explanation: 'Oblivious to the danger' (unaware/unconcerned) fits a person who keeps driving recklessly despite warnings; the other options mean the opposite.

relevance.note: Single filler 'oblivious' vs near-synonym distractors of opposite sense; standard PO filler

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences A–E to form a coherent paragraph.
A. As a result, many of them now offer collateral-free loans to small vendors.
B. Banks have traditionally been reluctant to lend to street vendors.
C. Digital payment records, however, now give lenders a window into a vendor's daily cash flows.
D. This is because such vendors rarely have documents showing a steady income.
E. Such data help lenders judge repayment capacity far more accurately than before.
questions.explanation: B introduces the problem, D gives the reason, C ('however') introduces the change, E explains how the data help, and A gives the result: B-D-C-E-A.

relevance.note: Five-sentence banking jumble with 'This is because'/'As a result' connectors; real PO format

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences A–E to form a coherent paragraph and identify the THIRD sentence.
A. Within weeks, the locality's waste was being sorted at source.
B. A group of residents decided to tackle the problem themselves.
C. The town's only landfill had been overflowing for years.
D. They began by distributing separate bins to every household.
E. The municipal body later adopted their model for the whole town.
questions.explanation: Order: C (problem) – B (residents act) – D (first step) – A (result) – E (adoption). The third sentence is D.

relevance.note: Find-THIRD-sentence jumble on civic theme; matches PO letter-option format

questions.question:
Choose the option that should replace the phrase in capitals to make the sentence correct.
IF I WOULD HAVE KNOWN about the delay, I would have taken another route.
questions.explanation: A third-conditional 'if' clause uses the past perfect: 'If I had known…, I would have taken…'. 'Would have' is not used in the if-clause.

relevance.note: Third conditional 'If I had known' replacement with plausible wrong tenses; good PO item

questions.question:
The table shows the number of laptops sold (in hundreds) by five stores in 2024 and 2025, and the percentage of the 2025 sales that were gaming laptops.
Store | 2024 | 2025 | Gaming % (2025)
P | 48 | 60 | 25%
Q | 36 | 45 | 40%
R | 52 | 40 | 20%
S | 40 | 50 | 30%
T | 64 | 56 | 25%

What is the percentage increase in the number of laptops sold by store Q from 2024 to 2025?

relevance.note: Table DI %-increase from two years; one-step, typical PO opener

questions.question:
The table shows the number of laptops sold (in hundreds) by five stores in 2024 and 2025, and the percentage of the 2025 sales that were gaming laptops.
Store | 2024 | 2025 | Gaming % (2025)
P | 48 | 60 | 25%
Q | 36 | 45 | 40%
R | 52 | 40 | 20%
S | 40 | 50 | 30%
T | 64 | 56 | 25%

What is the ratio of gaming laptops sold by P in 2025 to non-gaming laptops sold by S in 2025?
questions.explanation: P gaming = 25% of 60 = 15 hundred; S non-gaming = 70% of 50 = 35 hundred. Ratio 15 : 35 = 3 : 7.

relevance.note: Ratio of derived gaming/non-gaming values from % column, faithful PO table DI

What is the average number of laptops sold per store in 2024?

relevance.note: Simple average of a column in hundreds; fine as an easy DI set question

questions.question:
The table shows the number of laptops sold (in hundreds) by five stores in 2024 and 2025, and the percentage of the 2025 sales that were gaming laptops.
Store | 2024 | 2025 | Gaming % (2025)

questions.question:
A company has 1,200 employees in three departments — Sales, Tech and HR — in the ratio 5 : 4 : 3. Women make up 30% of Sales, 45% of Tech and 50% of HR.

What is the total number of women employees in the company?

relevance.note: Caselet with dept ratio and women %; total women; PO caselet format

questions.question:
A company has 1,200 employees in three departments — Sales, Tech and HR — in the ratio 5 : 4 : 3. Women make up 30% of Sales, 45% of Tech and 50% of HR.

What is the ratio of men in Sales to women in Tech?

relevance.note: Ratio men-Sales:women-Tech with reversed-ratio distractor 18:35

questions.question:
A company has 1,200 employees in three departments — Sales, Tech and HR — in the ratio 5 : 4 : 3. Women make up 30% of Sales, 45% of Tech and 50% of HR.

If 60 men are transferred from Sales to HR and nothing else changes, what percentage of HR employees will be women?
questions.explanation: HR becomes 300 + 60 = 360 employees with 150 women. 150/360 × 100 = 41⅔%.

relevance.note: Transfer-then-percentage caselet question, exactly the 'what changes after' trap

questions.question:
Solve and compare.
I. 2x² + 11x + 12 = 0
II. 3y² + 13y + 12 = 0
options: x = y or the relationship cannot be established

relevance.note: Negative fractional roots interleave -> CBE; classic PO quadratic trap

questions.question: Find the next term: 7, 8, 12, 21, 37, ?
questions.explanation: Differences are 1², 2², 3², 4², so the next difference is 5² = 25: 37 + 25 = 62.

relevance.note: Differences are consecutive squares; textbook PO missing series

questions.question: Find the wrong number in the series: 3, 7, 22, 88, 446, 2677

relevance.note: xn+1 with increasing n, 88 should be 89; PO wrong-series exactly

questions.question: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above its cost price and allows a discount of 15%. If his profit is ₹114, what is the cost price?

relevance.note: Markup-discount with profit amount -> CP; standard PO P&L

questions.question: Six years ago the ratio of the ages of P and Q was 5 : 7. Four years from now it will be 7 : 9. What is P's present age?

relevance.note: Past/future ratio ages, two equations; typical PO

questions.question: A starts a business with ₹24,000 and B joins at the same time with ₹36,000. After 4 months A invests another ₹12,000. Out of an annual profit of ₹25,500, what is B's share?

relevance.note: Partnership with mid-year top-up; standard PO arithmetic

questions.question: A can finish a job in 12 days and B in 18 days. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves and C joins B; B and C finish the remaining job in 2 days. In how many days can C alone finish the whole job?
questions.explanation: A+B in 4 days: 4(1/12 + 1/18) = 4 × 5/36 = 5/9. Remaining 4/9 in 2 days → B+C = 2/9 per day. C = 2/9 − 1/18 = 1/6 → 6 days.

relevance.note: A leaves, C joins, find C alone; typical PO time-work

questions.question: A 60-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 7 : 3. How many litres of water must be added to make the ratio 3 : 2?

relevance.note: Add water to change ratio; standard alligation

questions.question: A bag has 4 red, 5 blue and 3 green balls. Two balls are drawn at random. What is the probability that both are of the same colour?

relevance.note: Same-colour two balls via combinations; typical PO probability

questions.question:
Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G sit in a straight row, all facing north. D sits third from the left end. Only two persons sit between D and F. B sits at one of the extreme ends. Only one person sits between B and C. A is not an immediate neighbour of D. G sits somewhere to the right of E.

Who sits immediately to the right of G?
questions.explanation: Arrangement (left to right): A, E, D, G, C, F, B. D is 3rd; F is 6th; B must be at the right end (left end would put C on D's seat), so C is 5th; A cannot be 2nd or 4th so A is 1st; E is 2nd and G 4th. C is immediately right of G.

relevance.note: 7-person linear row facing north, unique arrangement AEDGCFB; PO-style though small

questions.question:
Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G sit in a straight row, all facing north. D sits third from the left end. Only two persons sit between D and F. B sits at one of the extreme ends. Only one person sits between B and C. A is not an immediate neighbour of D. G sits somewhere to the right of E.

How many persons sit between A and C?
questions.explanation: Arrangement: A, E, D, G, C, F, B. Between A (1st) and C (5th) are E, D and G — three persons.

relevance.note: Count-between question from same row, verified 3

questions.question:
Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G sit in a straight row, all facing north. D sits third from the left end. Only two persons sit between D and F. B sits at one of the extreme ends. Only one person sits between B and C. A is not an immediate neighbour of D. G sits somewhere to the right of E.

Which pair sits at the two extreme ends of the row?
questions.explanation: Arrangement: A, E, D, G, C, F, B — A and B are at the ends.

relevance.note: Extreme-ends pair question from same row

questions.question:
Seven persons J, K, L, M, N, O and P live on seven different floors of a building numbered 1 (bottom) to 7 (top). Each likes a different fruit — Apple, Banana, Cherry, Guava, Kiwi, Mango and Papaya. M lives on an odd-numbered floor above floor 4. Only two persons live between M and the one who likes Kiwi, who lives below M. L likes Mango and lives on an even-numbered floor. Only one person lives between L and N. N does not like Kiwi. O lives immediately above K. P likes Banana and lives on floor 1 or floor 2. J lives immediately above the one who likes Guava. The one who likes Apple lives on the top floor. The one who likes Papaya lives immediately below L.

Which fruit is liked by the person who lives immediately above O?
questions.explanation: Solution (floor 1→7): P-Banana, K-Kiwi, O-Papaya, L-Mango, M-Cherry, N-Guava, J-Apple. L (Mango) lives immediately above O.

relevance.note: 7-floor puzzle with fruit attribute, unique solution; strong PO floor puzzle

questions.question:
Seven persons J, K, L, M, N, O and P live on seven different floors of a building numbered 1 (bottom) to 7 (top). Each likes a different fruit — Apple, Banana, Cherry, Guava, Kiwi, Mango and Papaya. M lives on an odd-numbered floor above floor 4. Only two persons live between M and the one who likes Kiwi, who lives below M. L likes Mango and lives on an even-numbered floor. Only one person lives between L and N. N does not like Kiwi. O lives immediately above K. P likes Banana and lives on floor 1 or floor 2. J lives immediately above the one who likes Guava. The one who likes Apple lives on the top floor. The one who likes Papaya lives immediately below L.

How many persons live between K and N?
questions.explanation: K is on floor 2 and N on floor 6 (P-Banana 1, K-Kiwi 2, O-Papaya 3, L-Mango 4, M-Cherry 5, N-Guava 6, J-Apple 7). Three persons (O, L, M) live between them.

relevance.note: Persons-between from floor puzzle, verified K2/N6

questions.question:
Seven persons J, K, L, M, N, O and P live on seven different floors of a building numbered 1 (bottom) to 7 (top). Each likes a different fruit — Apple, Banana, Cherry, Guava, Kiwi, Mango and Papaya. M lives on an odd-numbered floor above floor 4. Only two persons live between M and the one who likes Kiwi, who lives below M. L likes Mango and lives on an even-numbered floor. Only one person lives between L and N. N does not like Kiwi. O lives immediately above K. P likes Banana and lives on floor 1 or floor 2. J lives immediately above the one who likes Guava. The one who likes Apple lives on the top floor. The one who likes Papaya lives immediately below L.

Who likes Cherry?
questions.explanation: M on 7 would need Kiwi on 4 (L's floor) – impossible, so M = 5 and Kiwi = 2. Apple is on 7. L (Mango) is on 4 or 6 with Papaya just below; L = 6 fails (N, J/Guava conditions), so L = 4, Papaya on 3, N on 6, J on 7 (Apple) with Guava (N) on 6. O–K and P fill 1–3: P-1 (Banana), K-2 (Kiwi), O-3 (Papaya). Remaining fruit Cherry goes to M.

relevance.note: Attribute lookup (Cherry=M) from floor puzzle

questions.question:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, all facing the centre. B sits third to the right of A. Only two persons sit between B and C. H sits second to the left of F. E is an immediate neighbour of both H and B. G sits immediately to the right of A.

Who sits third to the left of D?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from A: A, F, C, H, E, B, D, G. Facing the centre, left = clockwise. Third to the left of D: G, A, F → F.

relevance.note: 8-person circular facing centre, unique solution; PO standard

questions.question:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, all facing the centre. B sits third to the right of A. Only two persons sit between B and C. H sits second to the left of F. E is an immediate neighbour of both H and B. G sits immediately to the right of A.

What is the position of C with respect to G?
questions.explanation: Clockwise order: A, F, C, H, E, B, D, G. From G moving clockwise (left, facing centre): A (1st), F (2nd), C (3rd). So C is third to the left of G.

relevance.note: Relative position from circle (C is 3rd left of G)

questions.question:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H sit around a circular table, all facing the centre. B sits third to the right of A. Only two persons sit between B and C. H sits second to the left of F. E is an immediate neighbour of both H and B. G sits immediately to the right of A.

How many persons sit between A and E when counted from the right of A?
questions.explanation: Clockwise order: A, F, C, H, E, B, D, G. Moving to A's right (anticlockwise): G, D, B, then E. Three persons sit between them.

relevance.note: Count-from-right question; verified 3 between

questions.question:
Statements: All pens are books. Some books are bags. No bag is a chair.
Conclusions: I. Some pens are bags. II. Some books are not chairs.
questions.explanation: I: pens and bags have no definite link — only a possibility, so it does not follow. II: the books that are bags cannot be chairs, so some books are not chairs — follows.

relevance.note: 3-statement syllogism, chain via 'No bag is chair'; standard

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few cups are plates. All plates are spoons. No spoon is a knife.
Conclusions: I. Some cups are not knives. II. All cups being spoons is a possibility.
questions.explanation: 'Only a few cups are plates' → some cups are plates and some are not. Cups that are plates are spoons, hence not knives → I follows. The cups that are not plates may still be spoons, so 'all cups being spoons' is possible → II follows.

relevance.note: 'Only a few' with possibility conclusion; exactly PO 2024 trap

questions.question:
Statement: P > Q ≥ R = S < T
Conclusions: I. P > S  II. Q > T
questions.explanation: P > Q ≥ R = S gives P > S (I follows). Q ≥ S and T > S give no relation between Q and T (II does not follow).

relevance.note: Single-chain inequality, easy PO type

Statements: A ≥ B > C; D < C ≤ E; F > E

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

For most of the last century, bankers treated the weather as background noise. A failed monsoon might raise defaults in a few farm districts, but the damage was local and temporary, and lenders priced it in as ordinary risk. That comfortable assumption is now being questioned. Heatwaves that shut factories for weeks, floods that submerge entire industrial clusters and droughts that drain the reservoirs feeding power plants can impair borrowers across sectors at the same time. Because such shocks are correlated, a loan book that looks well diversified on paper may in fact be exposed to a single underlying hazard.

Regulators have begun to respond, though cautiously. Rather than prescribing capital charges straight away, many supervisors are first asking banks to measure their exposure: to map where their borrowers' assets are located, to estimate how a severe flood or a sharp rise in carbon prices would affect repayment, and to disclose these findings. Critics argue that such stress tests rely on models stretching decades into the future and are therefore little more than educated guesses. Supporters reply that an imperfect estimate is better than none, and that the very exercise forces boards to think about risks they once ignored.

There is also a quieter danger. If lenders respond to climate risk simply by withdrawing credit from vulnerable regions, they may deepen the hardship of communities that are already least able to adapt. The challenge, therefore, is not merely to protect balance sheets but to finance the transition — funding drought-resistant irrigation, resilient housing and cleaner industry — so that today's risky borrowers become tomorrow's safe ones.

Which of the following best captures the main idea of the passage?
options: Climate shocks are becoming a correlated, system-wide credit risk, and banks must measure it and finance adaptation rather than simply retreat
Regulators have already imposed heavy capital charges on loans exposed to climate risk
A failed monsoon is the single biggest cause of bad loans in the banking system
Climate stress tests are guesswork and should be abandoned by regulators
Banks should stop lending to drought-prone regions to protect their balance sheets
questions.explanation: The passage moves from correlated climate risk (para 1) to measuring it (para 2) to financing the transition instead of withdrawing credit (para 3). The other options are contradicted or are only partial details.

relevance.note: 350-word climate-risk banking passage, main-idea with retreat/overstatement traps

Which box is Green?
questions.explanation: Bottom to top: V (Black), R (White), T (Green), P (Red), U (Pink), Q (Yellow), S (Blue). T is Green.

relevance.note: 7-box stack with colour; unique solution

questions.question:
Seven boxes P, Q, R, S, T, U and V are kept one above another in a stack (position 1 is the bottom and 7 the top). Each box is of a different colour — Red, Blue, Green, Yellow, White, Black and Pink.
Box P is kept exactly in the middle of the stack. S is the Blue box and is kept above P, with only two boxes between S and P. Only one box is kept between Q and P, and Q is above P. The box immediately below S is Yellow. The Pink box is kept immediately above P. As many boxes are below T as are above U. T is kept below the Pink box. R is kept immediately above the Black box. The Green box is kept immediately above R. The White box is kept somewhere below the Red box.

How many boxes are kept between R and Q?
questions.explanation: R is at position 2 and Q at position 6, so T, P and U — three boxes — lie between them.

relevance.note: Boxes between R and Q verified 3

questions.question:
Seven boxes P, Q, R, S, T, U and V are kept one above another in a stack (position 1 is the bottom and 7 the top). Each box is of a different colour — Red, Blue, Green, Yellow, White, Black and Pink.
Box P is kept exactly in the middle of the stack. S is the Blue box and is kept above P, with only two boxes between S and P. Only one box is kept between Q and P, and Q is above P. The box immediately below S is Yellow. The Pink box is kept immediately above P. As many boxes are below T as are above U. T is kept below the Pink box. R is kept immediately above the Black box. The Green box is kept immediately above R. The White box is kept somewhere below the Red box.

What is the colour of the box kept immediately below U?
questions.explanation: U is at position 5; the box below it is P, which is Red.

relevance.note: Colour below U = Red

questions.question:
Statements: Some files are folders. All folders are drawers. No drawer is a shelf.
Conclusions: I. Some files are not shelves. II. All files being drawers is a possibility.
questions.explanation: The files that are folders are drawers and hence cannot be shelves, so I follows. Nothing prevents the remaining files from also being drawers, so the possibility in II also holds. Both follow.

relevance.note: Some/All/No with possibility, both follow

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few banks are lenders. All lenders are traders.
Conclusions: I. All banks being lenders is a possibility. II. Some traders are banks.
questions.explanation: 'Only a few banks are lenders' means some banks are definitely not lenders, so I cannot be possible. The banks that are lenders are traders, so some traders are banks — II follows.

relevance.note: 'Only a few' kills 'all being' possibility; PO trap

questions.question:
Statements: M > N ≥ O; P ≤ O < Q; R ≥ Q
Conclusions: I. M > P  II. R ≤ N
questions.explanation: M > N ≥ O ≥ P gives M > P, so I follows. R ≥ Q > O and N ≥ O give no relation between R and N, so II does not follow.

relevance.note: Three-statement inequality

questions.question:
Statements: A ≥ B = C > D; E ≤ C < F
Conclusions: I. B > E  II. B = E
questions.explanation: B = C ≥ E, so B ≥ E. Neither I nor II is definite alone, but together they cover every possibility (B > E or B = E). Either I or II follows.

relevance.note: Either-or complementary pair; PO standard

questions.question:
In a certain code, 'P # Q' means P is the mother of Q; 'P $ Q' means P is the brother of Q; 'P @ Q' means P is the wife of Q; and 'P & Q' means P is the son of Q.
If A $ B # C @ D & E, how is B related to D?
questions.explanation: B # C: B is C's mother. C @ D: C is D's wife. So B is the mother of D's wife — D's mother-in-law.

relevance.note: Coded blood relation with mother-in-law; PO type

questions.question:
Study the arrangement:
M 5 @ T 8 K # 3 B % 7 R & 2 Q E 9 $ H 4 L
How many letters are immediately preceded by a symbol and immediately followed by a number?
questions.explanation: Qualifying letters: T (@ T 8) and H ($ H 4). B is preceded by 3 and R by 7, which are numbers. Total = 2.

relevance.note: Letter preceded by symbol & followed by number

questions.question:
Numbers: 583  729  416  952  367
If the first and third digits of each number are interchanged, what is the difference between the largest and the smallest of the new numbers?
questions.explanation: New numbers: 385, 927, 614, 259, 763. Largest − smallest = 927 − 259 = 668.

relevance.note: Digit-swap number formation

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (1)?
questions.explanation: 'Out of reach' = not accessible, which is the point of the paragraph. 'Out of hand' means uncontrolled, 'out of touch' means unaware, 'out of order' means not working, and 'out of range' is used for signals or limits — all are real idioms that break the meaning here.

relevance.note: 'out of reach' collocation vs hand/touch/range look-alikes; typical IBPS PO 2024 cloze opener, slightly easy

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (2)?
questions.explanation: Moneylenders charge 'exorbitant' (unreasonably high) rates. 'Extravagant' describes spending, 'exuberant' describes cheerful energy, 'exhaustive' means thorough and 'extraneous' means irrelevant — look-alikes that do not collocate with 'rates of interest'.

relevance.note: exorbitant vs extravagant/exuberant/exhaustive ex- look-alikes - exactly the PO cloze distractor style

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (3)?
questions.explanation: Loans are 'disbursed' (paid out). 'Dispersed' means scattered, 'disbanded' is used for groups, 'disposed' needs 'of', and 'dismissed' means rejected — none describes paying out a loan.

relevance.note: disbursed vs dispersed/disbanded/disposed - classic banking-context look-alike set

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (4)?
questions.explanation: 'In the way sceptics had feared' — 'fear' can take the implied clause as its object. 'Alarmed', 'frightened', 'scared' and 'terrified' are verbs that need a person as object (sceptics had alarmed someone), so they make the sentence ungrammatical here.

relevance.note: only 'feared' takes a direct object after 'had'; synonym-set trap is PO-like though slightly unusual set of emotion words

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (5)?
questions.explanation: 'Risk + -ing' (they risk being left out) is the correct pattern. 'Threaten' takes 'to + verb', while 'endanger', 'menace' and 'imperil' need a noun object (endanger their chances), not a gerund describing what may happen to the subject.

relevance.note: 'risk being left out' (risk + gerund) vs threaten/endanger/imperil; good grammatical collocation trap

questions.question: Which word best fits blank (6)?
questions.explanation: Bringing cash-based firms into the formal system means efforts to 'formalise' the informal economy. 'Formulate' (draw up a plan), 'normalise', 'finalise' and 'fortify' are look-alikes that give no sensible meaning with 'the informal economy'.

relevance.note: formalise the informal economy vs formulate/normalise/finalise; strong look-alike cloze item

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Each of the branches has been asked to submit its quarterly figures by Friday.
Hardly had the auditors left than the manager called an emergency meeting.
The proceeds from the sale of the bonds was used to repay the loan.
Neither of the two proposals were found acceptable by the board.
The bank, as well as its two subsidiaries, have reported higher profits this year.
questions.explanation: 'Each of … has … its' is correct. Errors: 'Hardly … when' (not 'than'); 'proceeds' is plural, so 'were used'; 'Neither of the two proposals was'; with 'as well as' the verb agrees with the first subject 'The bank' → 'has reported'.

relevance.note: pick-correct-sentence with hardly..than, proceeds-was, neither-were, as well as-have traps; matches PO 2024/25 format

questions.question:
Which pair of the highlighted words should be interchanged to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct?
The slowdown in deposit growth has (A) forced banks to compete harder for (B) savers, (C) squeezing their funding costs and (D) pushing up the margins they earn on loans.
questions.explanation: Competing for savers raises (pushes up) banks' funding costs and squeezes their lending margins. Interchanging C and D gives '…pushing up their funding costs and squeezing the margins they earn on loans'.

relevance.note: word swap C-D: competition pushes up funding costs and squeezes margins; logic-based swap as in PO 2024

passages.title: Cloze passage: cash-flow lending to small firms
passages.text:
Read the passage carefully. Each numbered blank has a question below it.

For years, formal credit has remained largely out of (1) ______ for India's small manufacturers. Banks typically ask for property as collateral and for audited balance sheets, documents that many family-run units simply do not possess. The result is a persistent financing gap that pushes owners towards moneylenders who charge (2) ______ rates of interest.

A quieter change is now under way. With the customer's consent, lenders can pull verified data on GST filings, bank statements and digital receipts through account aggregators, and assess a firm on the strength of its cash flows rather than its fixed assets. Early evidence suggests that such loans are being (3) ______ in days rather than weeks, and that default rates have not risen in the way sceptics had (4) ______.

Yet the model has limits. Firms that still deal largely in cash leave thin digital footprints, and they (5) ______ being left out of the very system designed to include them. Policymakers will therefore need to pair data-driven lending with efforts to (6) ______ the informal economy, or the financing gap will merely shift rather than close.
